speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: SITUATION IN REGARD TO RHUBARB IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: I am in receipt of a telegram from some merchants in Weyburn, Saskatchewan, indicating a condition which may be prevalent in other cities of western Canada. They report that rhubarb is going to waste because there are no sugar permits available and consequently housewives are unable to make use of the rhubarb either for canning or for cooking purposes. Will the minister undertake to see that steps are taken immediately to deal with this unfortunate situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SITUATION IN REGARD TO RHUBARB IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
I regret that I cannot give the undertaking. I have gone very carefully into the question of rhubarb since I received notice of this question, and I find that provision was made for one pound of sugar per capita of the population of Canada for the purpose of cooking rhubarb alone. That one pound of sugar would be sufficient to cook five pounds of rhubarb, which would mean twenty-five pounds for a family of five. If more sugar
I Mr. Coldwell.]
is required for this purpose it will have to come out of the canning allotment or out of the ordinary sugar ration.

maintopic: SITUATION IN REGARD TO RHUBARB IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: The complaint is not that sugar is lacking but that the permits are not available. This is an important item of food for many people on the prairies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SITUATION IN REGARD TO RHUBARB IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to revert to my answer to the hon. member for Weyburn. I understood that he was asking for an increase in the sugar ration, but if it is merely a matter of administration I shall be glad to look into it at once.

speechtext:
I wish to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture. It is based on an article appearing in this morning's Journal, headed "Meat Board to Control Distribution". It contains a paragraph that reads:
The Canadian bacon board has been reconstituted as a meat board, with power to control distribution of all meat, Minister Gardiner announced last night.
The article as a whole is short and in my judgment it is not comprehensive enough; that is to say, it does not set out sufficiently the powers of the new board. First, may I ask the minister why this announcement was not made in the house, rather than in the manner in which it ha3 been made, seeing that the house is in session; and second, I should like to have the minister make a statement to the house outlining the powers of the new board, and informing the house whether these powers with regard to price ceiling and rationing, formerly under the wartime prices and trade board, are now being transferred to the new board so far as meat is concerned.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: RECONSTITUTION OF BACON BOARD-CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION
speechtext:
The terms of the order in council to all intents and purposes give the same powers to the new meat board as were previously
held by the bacon board, but their activities will now extend to beef as well as pork. It does not make any change with regard to the control which the prices board has over rationing and over the setting of prices. There is no change whatsoever in that regard. It is simply a reconstituting of the bacon board as a meat board, and while I did not make the announcement to -the house, I did mention it the other day in the committee on agriculture.

subtopic: RECONSTITUTION OF BACON BOARD-CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION
speechtext: Will the Minister of Agriculture lay on the table the order in council setting up the new board?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: RECONSTITUTION OF BACON BOARD-CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LAY-OFF BY CANADIAN INGERSOLL RAND COMPANY
speechtext: I want to thank my hon. friend for giving me notice of this question. I have a complaint to lay before the Minister of National Defence for Air in regard to delays in the delivery and receipt of cable messages to our boys in the air force in Britain. War Appropriation-Procedure

speakerposition: topic
subtopic
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago when we were discussing questions related to the business of the house and the order of procedure my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) mentioned to me across the floor of the house that he would ask the government to consider the question of allowing the Department of Labour to be considered next. My hon. friend at that time had reference to discussions under the war appropriation measure.
Two defence departments, namely those of the air and army, had made presentations. The army's presentation is now completed; that of the air force partly so; but there has not been at this time any presentation on the part of the navy. According to the original plan it was proposed that we should follow with the Department of Munitions and Supply, and then that upon a statement by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) we might discuss the question of man-power generally.
I replied to my hon. friend that I should like to consult with the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Labour before giving a final answer. I did say I would seek to oblige hon. members opposite, andi to meet their wishes as far as possible. I stated further at the time that I thought it was logical at least to continue discussions on the three defence departments, and my Hon. friend opposite agreed.
The question came up again yesterday, at which time I intimated that up to that time I had not had a chance to confer with my colleagues. I did so last night. Both the Minister of Munitions and Supply and the Minister of Labour feel that a much more effective and intelligent presentation of the whole man-power problem could be made to the house if the Minister of Munitions and Supply were to make his statement first, and be followed later by the Minister of Labour. I must say that after discussing the matter with them I agree with their view. The whole man-power problem will I believe become much more intelligible, for purposes of discussion in the house if that order is followed. I believe there would be an avoidance of repetition and unnecessary discussion, and also there would be better and more effective understanding in the country if we had before us in the first instance a full statement of the needs of the services and of
war industries. When the needs are presented to the house, then the Minister of Labour will be in a better position to deal more particularly with the manner in which those needs as well as others are being met and are to be met.
I am most anxious in every way to accommodate hon. members opposite, and I hope they will not think that I have anything in mind other than just what I have stated. This procedure will I hope materially shorten the discussion in the house, and would be not only the most logical method of presentation, but the most effective method of presentation of the whole problem. I mention this now in order that hon. members may understand the order in which we propose to proceed.
Up to the present the government has avoided introducing other measures, or bringing down new subjects for discussion while we have been dealing with the war appropriation bill. In some ways, that is a distinct disadvantage, because any discussion carried on for so many days at a time-even weeks at a time-soon becomes wearisome. On the other hand we have realized there is nothing the country is as much concerned about, or about which the government itself is so much concerned, as the war appropriation bill and the subjects to which it relates. We have felt we should not take any chances whatsoever of having other than the fullest discussion of that measure. I hope hon. members opposite will agree that the government in following the course I am suggesting is following the right one.
I might add that yesterday the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) took exception to the government's departing from the original proposal, and this would seem to indicate that at least all hon. members opposite are not in agreement in the matter of following a different procedure.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext: I may be under some misapprehension as to the agreement respecting the sequence of debates, but at the moment I know of no arrangement-at least I can recall none-whereby the Department of Munitions and Supply would follow directly after the Department of National Defence for Naval Services. However, I am not prepared to offer any challenge with respect to the accuracy of my understanding. I have stated my recollection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend is right. I have just spoken to my colleague the Minister of National De-

War Appropriation-Procedure
fence and he states that at the time the arrangement was made to which I first referred, when we discussed the matter with the leaders of the different parties,, the Department of Munitions and Supply was not mentioned. There was mention of only the three services.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
I thank the Prime
Minister for that statement, because that was my recollection. May I say at once that we cannot possibly meet my right hon. friend in this suggestion that the Department of Munitions and Supply should follow the Department of National Defence for Naval Services. There are good and sufficient reasons for this, one of which is that during the debate yesterday which was instituted by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) this whole matter was discussed. I would point out to the Prime Minister that the understanding had a direct bearing on the progress of that debate. During the debate the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 3283 of Hansard:
A day or two ago it was understood that after we completed the statements of the ministers of defence we might take as the next order of business the question of man-power, even before going into matters pertaining to the Department of Munitions and Supply. I do not think it will be very long before we reach the discussion of man-power, and the question of agricultural labour and the measures necessary to meet the needs of agriculture inevitably will come up as soon as that discussion is entered upon.
Then the right hon. gentleman went on to indicate what he has indicated this afternoon, and in referring to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) he said:
However, I think he may take it for granted that in so far as it may give promise of expediting the business of the house, we will seek to meet the wishes of the opposition in the matter.
If I may say to the Prime Minister, that had a very direct bearing upon the debate yesterday.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext: How?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
If the Minister of
Pensions and National Health will be as patient as he is sometimes, but not always,
I will answer his question, because I was just about to come to that point. The reason -why it had a bearing on the debate yesterday was that the discussion instituted by the hon. member for Temiscouata was only a piecemeal discussion of the whole problem of man-power. On another occas-sion in the house, after the Department of National Defence had been completed, I

mentioned to the Prime Minister that we were somewhat handicapped as a party in dealing with the whole problem of manpower because the Minister of Labour had not given his statement. We did not want to be dealing with this matter department by department, and it was largely because of that that this party did not take more than a token part in the discussion yesterday in order to make our position clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext: Ini any case the debate could not last beyond eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
In my opinion that had
nothing to do with our taking part in the debate. We had the statement of the Prime Minister, which perhaps was not a guarantee, that the Minister of Labour would come on, and it left the definite impression that the manpower problem, would not be delayed and the whole picture would be laid before us. Certainly it was my understanding that he would come on before the Minister of Munitions and Supply.
As I said last night, in my opinion the problem of manpower in Canada is the major issue facing the Canadian people. The hon. member for Temiscouata raised only part of this problem; the whole problem must be dealt with. I understood the Prime Minister's argument this afternoon to- be that we should have the services and their demands and requirements before us, that we should have the demands and requirements of the Department of Munitions and Supply before us, and that we should then go on with the Minister of Labour. If that argument were followed to its logical conclusion, we should have the Department of Agriculture before the man-power problem was actually discussed by the Minister of Labour.
I must take very strong exception to the suggestion made. I realize that the government has it in its power to arrange the sequence of business in connection with the war appropriation measure, but I submit to the government that it is a mistaken procedure to have the Department of Munitions and Supply follow the Department of National Defence for Naval Services. That would mean that we should be considerably further along with the session. On a previous occasion, I think in February or March, the Minister of Labour made a partial statement on manpower but-

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
You would not let him
go on.

War Appropriation-Procedure

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
I do not know whether
my hon. friend means that as an, interruption.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
You would not let him
finish his statement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
I think the Minister of
Labour should be given the opportunity to complete his statement which he gave partly on a previous occasion. So far as I can see there is no justification for a further postponement of the discussion of this problem which is so vital to this country. We should come to grips immediately with this manpower problem; we should not be delayed by having to take another department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
I hope I have made it quite clear that the government's desire is to expedite the business of the house and, with its knowledge of what has to be presented, it is I think in the best position to say how the complete picture can most effectively be presented to the house, presented that is, in a manner that will be most helpful to a discussion in the house. The desire to have the Minister of Munitions and Supply follow the defence departments has been entirely that of getting before the house the full picture of the requirements of the different defence forces and war industries. The question of farm, labour comes of course into it.
If it will help to avoid any misunderstanding between us and enable the house to reach the manpower discussion more rapidly than might otherwise be possible, I may say to my hon. friend that I am quite prepared to suggest to my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply, that he make his statement which will set forth the essential features of the work of the Department of Munitions and Supply during the past year-I imagine that this statement may take two or three hours, but not more than that-and that he then allow the discussion on the statement to stand over until there has been a discussion of the man-power problem upon the statement of the Minister of Labour.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext: Why does my right hon. friend suggest that the Minister of Munitions and Supply make his statement before the Minister of Labour makes his?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext: For the reason that the house will wish to know what manpower has been employed during this past year, is now being employed and will be required from now on in the war industries of the country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext: That may not come out except by cross-examination during the debate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
With all due respect to my hon. friend, recalling What the Minister of Munitions and Supply has said in previous years, I think we may assume that he will follow a similar line of procedure this year, and give to the house a very full statement with respect to the man-power required by the war industries. I do not see how a discussion on man-power can proceed intelligently or without a great deal of repetition unless that statement is made in the first instance. For that reason I hope that my hon. friend will acquiesce in this proposal. I make it because apparently there has been some difference of view between us and I am anxious to accommodate both sides of the house as far as I can.
With regard to the needs of agriculture, may I say that we had a debate on the question of the shortage of farm labour earlier in the session. At that time a formal motion was made and a debate took place upon the question. Under the rules of this house a second debate cannot take place on a question once it has been discussed and disposed of. I have not raised that point although it might have been raised yesterday. I simply point it out as an additional reason why the government, in controlling the business of the house, should follow the sequence that it feels to be necessary and desirable.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has asked me if I would be ready to acquiesce in his last suggestion. This last suggestion is very important because when he raises the question about the shortage of agricultural labour having been debated before in the house, it then forms part of the whole picture. The difficulty that we have been faced with from the beginning is that matters are being dealt with piecemeal. We have always had that difficulty. What we are trying to get as quickly as possible is a discussion of the whole problem of man-power. It is suggested that the Minister of Munitions and Supply make his statement and then further discussion stand over until the man-power problem has been disposed of. At the moment I am not able to assess accurately the position in which we may find ourselves with respect to dealing with the Department of Munitions and Supply. I am afraid we cannot acquiesce in the suggestion of the Prime Minister, but the matter is in his hands.
Mr. M. J. COLDW'ELL (Rosetown-Biggar): Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word on this, if I may. It seems to me that the logical procedure is the one outlined by the Prime Minister in the first instance, that we have statements from the three defence de-
War Appropriation-Procedure

partments and from Munitions and Supply, because then we would be in a position intelligently to discuss matters. I felt that yesterday, and I feel it even more strongly to-day. The suggestion made by the Prime Minister to have the Minister of Munitions and Supply make a statement and then leave that in abeyance while we discuss the Depart-of Labour would lead to the defeat of the objective we had in view when we agreed to a discussion of the war appropriation bill department by department, because of necessity the figures presented by the Minister of Munitions and Supply would have a close bearing on matters coming within the Department of Labour. The two departments might almost be discussed interchangeably. If we are to follow the procedure outlined by the Prime Minister it might be better to take those two departments and discuss them together because they are so closely interrelated. Personally, as I said yesterday, I think the logical order is the order originally suggested, to take the Department of Munitions and Supply and then the Department of Labour. Then we shall know the labour problems arising out of all the war departments.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext: My hon. friend the leader of the opposition has quite rightly said that the responsibility is on the government and particularly on myself. I have made a suggestion to him which I thought would be helpful but he is not prepared to accept it. The hon. leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation says that he thinks the suggestion is illogical and should not be followed. We will then proceed with the statement of the Minister of Labour.

speechtext: All right.

speechtext: I offered to answer all the questions which have been put to me in the last two days. If the committee does not want me to answer these questions to-day, I take it that the committee wants to make speeches, and I will listen. I shall be on the other end; that is all.
The alternative is that the minister himself will make a little speech in which he will answer the questions. I would be in favour of having the minister answer questions in a speech.
The minister last evening gave me the opportunity, which I appreciate, of going over the new contracts with respect to the air observer and elementary flying training schools.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That had better come under another item, had it not? There is an item just for civilian schools.
If that is so, I will not continue.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Well, this is a general discussion, of course.
Surely; go ahead.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: All right.

I have a number of questions to ask arising out of this matter. The minister very kindly, as I stated, had a comparison made between the old contracts covering elementary flying training and air observer schools and the new contracts covering these schools. I have taken the opportunity of perusing the' contracts, and any objection which I have heretofore expressed to the operation of these schools generally is removed by the amendments to the contracts during the present year. There are however some matters which I think still could be improved upon.
I will outline in general so far as the elementary training schools are concerned the previous arrangements which were in effect. There was paid to the flying training companies a certain amount during each period of four weeks for maintenance. In addition there was a considerable profit allowed per flying hour. Amendments have been now made by which considerable reductions have taken place in the management fee; it is now entirely eliminated except so far as actual expenses are concerned. As to the saving or loss on operations, up to the time of the new agreement the crown has paid seventy-five per cent and the company twenty-five per cent, and under the new arrangements the division will be eighty per

War Appropriation-Air Services
cent and twenty per cent. Generally speaking the result will effect considerable savings in the operations of these schools. There are however some changes which I think might still be made, and I place them before the minister.
The first I have in mind is in connection with insurance to take the place of the workmen's compensation act insurance in effect in the various provinces. I have not the available figures now, but if my memory is correct the amount paid by each of these schools per month averages about $1,100. I speak subject to correction in that regard. There are ten air observer schools and some twenty elementary flying training schools in Canada. At the present time the insurance is carried by insurance companies. It covers the personnel of these various schools who have not available to them the protection granted under the provincial workmen's compensation acts. I ascertained, as a result of our investigation some two years ago into these items, that the amount which was being disbursed by way of compensation was about twenty per cent of the actual amount of the premiums. With the government receiving the profits at the conclusion of the contracts for disposal as indicated in the two contracts, a saving running well on to $150,000 a year could be effected if the government itself would assume the responsibility and liability for compensation to the employees.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member if he lias thought this thing through? Would it mean the setting up of a sort of new insurance department by the government just for these schools? I have not thought it through.

No. In each of these schools there is already sufficient staff fpr the purpose. All the government would have to do would be from time to time, as accidents take place, deduct from the amount paid by each of the schools the equivalent amount now paid to the insurance companies sufficient to be disbursed among those who suffer injury and accident. In fact, the statement I make as to the savings is, I know, having regard to past payments, a considerable underestimate of the saving which could take place. In that connection I wish to ask the following questions: the amount paid during the past year for insurance premiums in the various schools; the amount paid by each school per year; and the names of the agents with whom the said insurance is placed.
My next point is in connection with the cost per flying hour-including oil and gas-in the air observer schools. I should think there would have been a large reduction in that
[Mr. Diefenbaker.)
connection. In 1941 the costs amounted to $5.68 per hour, which I submit could be greatly reduced. I would like to have the figures for the various schools.
The next matter I want to take up is that of 'catering. Under the old agreements the amounts which were allowed per pupil for staff amounted to ninety cents a day, and in most cases it was done by catering companies such as Crawley & McCracken Company Limited and George Coles Limited. The criticism I previously made of this item was that too much was being paid to these companies and that a considerable saving could take place; and I notice in the new agreement a saving which I compute at ajpout ten per cent.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: About ten cents a day, is it not?
From now on there is the 50-cent rate in place of the rate which heretofore applied.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: But we have to pay the army for the rations which they supply. That would be about 40 cents. That is 90 cents instead of a dollar.
At any rate, it is a very considerable saving-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is a saving.

-and along the line which has been indicated. I should like to have a statement showing the cost to graduate pupils in the air observer schools and elementary flying schools. The original amount was estimated at $1,653.57, but with the change under the new agreement I should like to get the figures in that connection.
In the press recently there was a statement to the effect that a considerable change had taken place with respect to the capital stock of the companies concerned. It was stated that the common stock had been called in, and I suggest that a statement in that regard would clear up many misconceptions touching the holding of stock. Under the arrangements with the elementary training schools, in most instances these schools were brought into being by flying clubs and sponsored1 by them. There are two or three of these schools, however, that are under private ownership.

speechtext:
One elementary school, I
believe-Three Rivers.

There	are two
others, if my memory is correct, that were not directly sponsored by flying clubs. These flying clubs have secured large amounts of money in the form of surpluses, which are being held1 until the conclusion of the war by the various companies operating the schools,

War Appropriation-Air Services
at which time allocations will be made to the flying clubs that have sponsored the several schools, or such other disposition will be made of the moneys as may be determined by the minister.
Some indication of the profits which these elementary flying training schools have made was shown in a return, sessional paper 326, brought down in answer to a number of questions asked by myself on April 26 last. I am not going over the record of these profits in detail, but I have a suggestion to make as to the use that might very well be made of these moneys. Taking the schools in the order in which they appear, the answer is that profits, before making provision for income and excess profits tax, including the company's share of operation and maintenance savings, are fairly substantial. Take the first one, Fort William. For the first period of twenty-four weeks the amount was $16,732; for the second period $14,547; for the third period, $11,636; for the fourth period, $11,105. Then it falls away in the sixth period to $6,025.
Take Prince Albert, Saskatchewan. In the first period; the amount was $9,589; then $12,166, $10,360, $3,392, $8,703, and $202. There are others but I will not refer to them by name. There are some in larger amounts- $19,000 surplus and profit during the period of twenty-four weeks; another, $25,300; another, $15,000; another, $26,900; and so on. These amounts are held, less the payment of course of income tax and excess profits tax, to the end of the war.
Mr. POWER; They have paid in $1,370,000. They are being made to give that eighty per cent to us now.
The minister says it is now being paid, but there is nothing to indicate that this was being done.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I d'o not think that was in the contract; my hon. friend is right. I have not seen anything in the contract, but we did have the right at any time to ask for a certain portion. Perhaps not the whole eighty per cent, but a large portion has been paid and the amounts come to $1,370,000.
That was a suggestion I made repeatedly.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Quite right.

I believe that to be one way in which these moneys could be controlled. On the other hand, in the operation of the air observer schools large profits are being made which will revert to the crown. As a result of the establishment of these civilian schools a large amount of money
will be available after the war for aviation purposes, and I think that money might very well be used in the continuance of aviation facilities, in their extension, and to aid in the establishment of a post-war aviation scheme applicable to the British commonwealth of nations.
The other day a question was asked the Prime Minister as to whether or not conversations had been initiated between the United Kingdom and the self-governing dominions with respect to an empire plan for post-war civil aviation, to which the answer was no. To-day the British people and the British parliament itself, within the past two weeks, have been debating this question. An opportunity should) be given to men who serve in the air force to become rehabilitated after the conclusion of hostilities, and it is my opinion that these moneys that now revert to the crown, already totalling a considerable sum, which will become increasingly larger as the years go by, and the facilities that are now being operated by these schools, belonging to the crown, might very well form the basis for the establishment in Canada of a basis for an empire scheme. I believe the civilian schools and the whole set-up in the old country will be utilized for the same purpose, and it is time for us ini Canada to give the lead in this direction. It would benefit the men when they return after the war from service in the air force, to continue in this as a life work. Many of them will desire to do so and they should have that opportunity, and for this reason among others, we should' now lay the foundations for such an all-empire air transport service.
A few days ago there appeared in the press an item setting out the attitude of the British people towards this matter. Canada has not yet participated in a conference regarding this poshwar scheme with the other nations within the commonwealth of nations. I think she should, in order to establish, as it were, an all-family round-the-world transport system for the purpose of uniting still more the various nations of the empire, and, in addition to that, affording an opportunity to ensure to the men who serve in the air force jobs and positions when they return. Recently the Sunday Times dealt with this matter, and if I may be permitted I should like to quote what it said in an editorial; with this I shall conclude. In Great Britain there has been a most favourable reaction toward the establishment of this empire air transport system. As yet in Canada opinion has not been crystallized and there have been no representations made by Canada to the other empire nations, if I correctly understand the Prime Minister's



War Appropriation-Air Services
statement. I do think now is the time to lay the foundation for the continuance of this empire after the war, to bind it together more closely than ever before by the establishment of an empire air transport plan. In that connection I shall refer to the editorial, which sums up the attitude generally of the British people:
London is now only eighteen hours from New York, ten hours from Cairo, eight hours from Moscow. Even the great ocean barrier of the Pacific is flown regularly many times a week at two hundred miles an hour or more.
Air communication will play a major part in the lives of nations from now forward. Public discussions on both sides of the Atlantic are ahead of official thought, and reveal such weight of enterprise that international agreements on the air routes of the world are a pressing concern.
A primary British need to-day is for a policy for empire air transport. At present there is none. R.A.F. transport command is doing invaluable work as a military unit. To suggest it should assume other than military functions in operating world air routes would be to court disaster.
There is a strong case for starting now _ to design transport planes . . . but civil aviation will offer such a vast field for enterprise after the war that there seems to be no justification for restricting it to monopolistic control-unless the greater goal of full internationalization can be achieved, with all its manifest benefits.
Then, it goes on to say that the British dominions and India should be parties to an Anglo-American understanding. My submission, Mr. Chairman, is that while in the past I have not always seen eye to eye in regard to the turning over to civilian companies of the elementary and air observer training of our air force, the results achieved have been tremendous. We have built up airfields and communications across Canada which will form a foundation upon which Canada can offer a great contribution toward an empire transport system. I think the minister now should lay plans, and should tell the people of Canada what those plans are, with reference to the use of our aerodromes and other facilities when the war is over, whether they will be still controlled by the government or whether it is the intention to turn them over to private companies.
I do not know that there are any other matters with which I want to deal. So far as the air observer schools and the elementary flying training schools are concerned, the new contracts do away with many of the things to which previously I took objection. I realize that while experience was being secured, naturally some portions of the agreement were not what they should have been, but I do think the minister is entitled to every commendation for having made the

alterations to some of which I have referred to-day.
There is just one other point to which I should like to refer; that is the reclamation of oil in these various schools. To-day, with the shortage of oil that exists, everything possible should be done in the reclamation, of oil. I know the figures so far as one school is concerned. The total value of the oil that would have been wasted at that school if a reclamation plant had not been set up was $4,104. A reclamation plant was set up at a cost of only $957, and it brought about the saving of $3,200 worth of oil within the first year. As I understand it, some of the schools do not have reclamation plants as yet, but I think for the small expense involved and the very large savings that are brought about, consideration should be given to the setting up of reclamation plants and units at each of these schools.

May I ask the minister
if the airfields which have been constructed either by or for his department across Canada and into the north permit the landing of planes carrying ten tons?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am sorry I cannot answer my hon. friend. The elementary flying fields were not built for the operation of heavy types of planes, nor were the service flying fields. I do not know about ten tons, whether it is or is not a particularly heavy load. I know some of the planes weigh thirty and forty tons. I shall make inquiries, but offhand I could not say. I can tell my hon. friend that only a very small portion of our aerodromes are built for heavy machines. The elementary fields are built for the operation of light planes, generally speaking, and that is also the case in regard to the sendee flying fields.
I have read that the heaviest load carried by the planes flying north to-day is six thousand pounds, or three tons, but that the United States bombers going to Alaska-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
My hon. friend is talking about the aerodromes built for the purposes of the training plan. Normally they are not built for the operation of large transport planes, but aerodromes built for the purposes of these transport planes are capable of taking those planes carrying normal loads, and I should say possibly the ones to which he is referring are in that category.
Mr: MacNICOL: Then may I ask if the airfield being built northeast of the Pas-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I would not know.

It is not under your department?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall inquire, but I could not say offhand.
I understand that heavy bombing planes land there.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If they land there I presume it is built to accommodate such planes, but I could not say offhand whether a specific aerodrome would be capable of handling a plane carrying a ten ton load or a twenty ton load or a thirty ton load. I am not a technician, but I can tell my hon. friend that staging aerodromes, or aerodromes used for offensive or defensive purposes, normally can take almost any kind of plane. The ones built for elementary training take elementary training aircraft, which are light aircraft.

I was interested the other day when the minister indicated that he was in favour of granting commissions to as many of our young men as were qualified for them, regardless of quotas or any other ulterior motive or consideration. I wanted to raise a question in that regard. I have been told that boys who accept commissions are frequently a good deal worse off financially, after receiving their commissions, because of certain requirements made of them.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is correct.
And which they find unavoidable.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The income tax.
No, not the income tax; certain things incidental to the dignity of their craft, so to speak. Is that so?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is true.

Would I be in order if I were to ask the minister if that is the best way to have it? Would it not be better if the income of these boys was graduated so that the young man receiving a commission would not be worse off financially, and so that he could break even?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
There does seem to be quite a discrepancy now between the pay of a sergeant .pilot and that of a commissioned officer. I would hesitate to raise the pay of a commissioned officer without raising that of the sergeant pilot, and in that way we would be back to the place we started. I do not know what answer I can make to the question. Upon reading some literature from the United Kingdom government on this question I find they make the statement that a great many of their non-commissioned pilots do not wish 72537-2121
to become officers because of the financial loss involved. I .really do not know how I can grade these rates of pay in order to make it more attractive for someone to get a commission than to remain as a sergeant. I have no objection to looking into the matter, but I am afraid, if I may say so offhand, that my hon. friend is barking up the wrong tree.

The minister is quite right in his anxiety about the matter. In my view no consideration of financial reward should be troubling any of our prospective officers. I know of young men who in my opinion ought to be officers, because of the services they could render, but who, because of what to some people might be considered minor considerations, are deterred from going ahead.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Some men have refused commissions-not very many, actually, but some. But some warrant officers class 1 who are receiving equipment allowance would rather remain non-commissioned officers than accept commissions.
In any effort the minister makes which will result in our best boys becoming officers without their having to suffer anxiety because of financial arrangements, he will have my unswerving support.

speechtext:
He could talk to his
commanding officer or his immediate commander, but he would not be in any category which would necessitate our consulting him if we were going to move him.
What is the approximate number on the waiting list for air force?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Aircrew?
Yes.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I cannot tell the hon. member the number on the waiting list.
Approximately?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No, I cannot.
I understand there are quite a number.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: At this time there are fewer than there were. Is my hon. friend asking in connection with farm work?

No. That brings me to a question brought up the other day, as to why it was we are not training more in the air force. I do not wish the minister to misunderstand me, because I am not trying to criticize his efforts in connection with the air force. As I said yesterday, I think his attitude is the proper one. But I have been talking to officers in the air force and their complaint was that they could train more men if they had the facilities at hand. They pointed out an insufficiency of training aircraft. I do not know whether we have not the training aircraft, or whether we

have not the facilities in connection with air fields. Would the minister make a statement?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I can tell my hon. friend right away that we have a plant which is supposed to turn out a certain output of so many aircrew per annum. We have to build up our plant to its full capacity, and we are not proposing to increase it very much more. One very good reason is that we would not get the raw material if we kept on increasing it indefinitely, because there are not in Canada -I think I said this in my preliminary statement-an unlimited number of men fit for aircrew. I do not know yet; I may find out, to my cost, before I am through, that perhaps we have built a plant too big for the number of aircrew we may be able to get, as days go on. We are not being curtailed by lack of aircraft, and at this time we are not being curtailed by lack of aircrew.
Will the minister give consideration to giving airmen on sick leave extra time to get to and from their homes? It is a pressing point in British Columbia.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That would be purely a medical matter, if they are on sick leave. The medical man would state how long the sick leave would last, and each case would be dealt with on its merits.
For example, I have in mind a man who has been in hospital for some months, and at the expiration of that time will be given some furlough.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It depends on his condition, does it not?

Men from British Columbia who have been in hospital in Ontario or the maritime provinces find some difficulty; for they have only a few days at home. The suggestion has been made that they should be allowed the time to travel to and from their homes.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Surely the medical man must take into consideration the injuries that have been received. I should be very glad to have particulars of any case of that kind.
- Mr. GREEN: These men ought to be spending more of their time at home rather than on the train. I raised this question with the Minister of National Defence when his estimates were before us and he told me that he would discuss it with the minister. I think if the minister will look into this situation he will find that there is some hardship.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
There cannot be any such thing as a uniform sick leave. A man may

War Appropriation-Air Services
have a certain disability and he is told to go away to recuperate. This period of recuperation will be longer for one disability than for another. I cannot imagine the medical men saying to a man, "You are sick and are going to get two weeks' leave," and then saying the same thing to a man who is recovering from a really serious illness.
No, but I believe that once men in the air force are discharged from hospital they are given a sick furlough, either twelve or fourteen days.

I received a letter from a man who has two sons in the air force. Another son was called up recently under the provisions of the National Resources Mobilization Act and he now wishes to be transferred to the air force. There are a number of men in the army who are available for service only in Canada and who would like to transfer to the air force, but the opportunity is denied them. Apparently they are not permitted to make this transfer once they have been enrolled under the provisions of the mobilization act.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Before they actually enrolled, or whatever you call it, in the army they had the opportunity of going to the air force and volunteering for active service anywhere in the world. I will admit that there is no clear procedure laid down to provide for transfers from the army to the air force. Of course, if the army were willing to discharge them and they had the necessary qualifications for aircrew, we should be glad to have them.

One would think
that if there are men who are not willing to serve overseas in the army and who have the qualifications and are desirous to serve anywhere in the air force, the opportunity should be given to them to transfer.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They had that opportunity when they were first called up.

I appreciate that
but many of them did not realize their exact position.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall be glad to take that up with my colleague the Minister of National Defence. If there are any men who have not been willing to volunteer for active service overseas with the army and who would be willing to volunteer to go anywhere as aircrew, I should be glad to get them.

Is
there a sea rescue service in the R.C.A.F.?

Are awards given only to the non-commissioned ranks in this service?

understand that in Great Britain awards are given only to the non-commissioned ranks. Does that apply to the R.C.A.F.?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I should not think so, but I can inquire about that. It would be extraordinary in our service if we limited awards to non-commissioned officers or to other ranks. Is the limitation downward or upward?
Downward.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

It was stated ini the British Hansard that officers do not get them.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

There are certain awards
which are not given to officers, and there are other awards which are not given to other ranks. This distinction applies through the whole service. The D.S.O. is not given to other ranks and the D.C.M. is not given to officers. The Military Medal is not given to officers and the Military Cross is not given to other ranks.
The way I read the British Hansard an officer in that service canot get an award; they are given only to the non-commissioned officers and other ranks.

3. Travel, transportation and freight, $20,838,068.

Would it be possible to do anything to reduce the amount of unnecessary travelling that sometimes takes place? I do not know what the experience of other hon. members has been, but in travelling back and forth across the country I have talked to many men in the

War Appropriation-Air Services
air force who seem to have done a lot of unnecessary travelling. I realize that this is not an easy thing to eliminate. Sometimes it is caused by red tape, and sometimes it has not been easy to plan ahead. I came across one glaring example, but this is not by any means an isolated one. This young man had graduated as a member of aircrew in the east and he was told to go home to Moose Jaw on leave and then to come back, when he would be posted. After his leave he came back to eastern Canada and was posted to Mossbank, which is just a few miles outside of Moose Jaw. As I say, I realize that it is not always easy to eliminate this sort of thing, but I should like to know whether it has been drawn to the minister's attention. In view of the congestion on our railroads, every effort should be made to reduce unnecessary travelling.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: In the earlier days this was particularly bad, but I think it has improved lately. On my first trip to the Pacific coast I was astounded to find that most of the men there-in those days we had a surplus of aircrew and many of these men were on guard duty-had been enlisted in Nova Scotia. Some of them were as far away as Prince Rupert. There was a great deal of confusion in posting, but we have done our best to eliminate that. In the days of our early expansion, when pupils finished the elementary school training we wanted to fill up the service flying training school and we took them from almost anywhere, from the east and the west. I think in all commands to-day there are all categories of schools except the advanced training school. Probably the man referred to by the hon. member was shipped down east because they expected to send him overseas, and it may have been found that he would make a better instructor and they decided to send him to Mossbank. There has been and probably still is more travelling than there should be. I have done everything I can to eliminate it and will continue to do everything I can, because it is a serious problem.

One of the complaints that has reached me has to do with the women who are joining the air force. It has been pointed out that if a girl desires to train as a wireless operator and enlists in Vancouver or New Westminster, she may be sent to Toronto or Montreal. Then when she completes her training the girl from the west is usually posted in the east, while the girl from the east is posted in the west. When a girl posted in Halifax earns leave she finds it will take twelve or thirteen days

of her leave to go to the west coast and return. Could not a wireless school be established in British Columbia, and could not girls and men from the west be posted in the western provinces?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
It would be pretty difficult
to do that. We have a certain number of wireless schools established, I believe four. At one of them, in Montreal, we took out most of the men who were learning wireless operating, ground, and placed women there. There are not very many come in at each intake per month. We find it very difficult to establish another school, except at great cost; and even if we did, we might find that we could not take care of the output because there is a limited number of positions for wireless operators, ground, in Canada. The women who take up that course are mostly destined to remain in Canada.

break-down of this item for travel, transportation and freight?

I should not be surprised to learn that the minister had been working industriously to get free transportation for the men in the air force on embarkation leave and on furlough. Am I correct in my supposition?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I am afraid I have to say
that I adhere to the established policy for the three services, which is not quite free transportation on embarkation leave. I have a long statement here on leave. It is similar to that which was given in connection with the army. We have a joint committee for army, navy and air force before which we

War Appropriation-Air Services
thresh out any suggestion- of discrimination as between the three services. All three services follow the same rule as to leave.

I do believe that we should give free transportation, on embarkation leave and on, at least one furlough, no matter where the men may be stationed. As matters are now, the boys who come from poor families are at a disadvantage because all the money they can spare is used to help their folks. The result is that many are not able to go on leave. I think this matter should be taken up in the interests of justice.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That matter was thoroughly discussed when the army estimates were before the committee. I do not know that there is anything I can add. I think the Minister of National Defence said that he was going to give the matter further consideration. I have no objection to taking it up again at defence council, where the three services meet and discuss their common problems, to see what we can do about it.
I urge the minister to take it up and use all the pressure he can to put it through.
The minister will recall that a couple of days ago I asked about radio technicians. Can he make a statement now on that?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I have the answer here but it will take some time to read it. Perhaps it would be as well if we got on the record all the questions that are to be asked so that we could have the week-end to work over them. If not, I will answer now the questions we have at present.

My colleague the member for Cape Breton South was called out of the house but he has one matter to bring up which I will mention and perhaps the minister will give the information. It is a complaint from a man in the air force who joined at Sydney, Nova Scotia, was moved to Halifax and then to Toronto. He claims in his letter he was three nights on the train without any berth and no meals supplied. He is under the impression, whether it is correct or not I do not know, that when men move west of Toronto they are supplied with meals and berths. But the writer of this letter says that these men who came to Toronto from the maritimes got no meals or berths and on the last night they had to stand up in the day coach. This man certainly seemed to have had an unfortunate experience.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If it is a trip of only one night he does not get a berth. There is no distinction made between travelling east and west of Toronto. I think the Minister of National Defence made a statement on this question with reference to the army. The same thing applies to the air force. We get the same treatment as the others.
This is a man in the air force, not the army.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They do not get a berth if they are travelling only one night. If it is more than that I cannot say at the moment what accommodation they get, but there is no regulation that prohibits a man from getting a berth. I think he would be entitled to one if he was travelling more than one night. I am informed that it is in the regulations that he should get one. If he did not, he should have made his complaint to the proper authorities.
He was three nights on the train and got no berth and no meals.
I understand that members of the women's division are provided with berths, the same as in the army.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We changed the rule some time ago.
They get a berth if they are travelling only one night?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.
How is the amount spent on transportation divided between the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railways?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not think I have that information here, but I can get it for my hon. friend. It is about fifty-fifty.

Perhaps the minister will include those figures in his general statement on Monday. I have another question. Is any of the freight from central Canada to the maritimes routed through the United States on American lines? Jf so, how much?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will look that up.
I have had one or two bitter complaints from Nova Scotia and one from New Brunswick that too much freight was being routed through the United States at the expense of Canadian railways.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
My hon. friend is probably thinking of the short line through Maine to Saint John, New Brunswick, instead of going around by the Canadian National.

War Appropriation-Air Services
Yes.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We will check on that.
Many people in the maritimes feel that this is discrimination against them.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I spent a lot of time in that section of the country, and I can assure my hon. friend that freight trains there are passing so frequently that I think that is about all the traffic the Canadian National Railways can bear. That is, I would think so as a mere spectator.

This vote for capital expenditure is approximately S93i millions. It is true that is a reduction from the amount spent last year, but it is a very large amount of money. Is any provision made for checking the types of buildings that are being put up for the air force, for example, the equipment depots? I have had complaints to the effect that they are far more expensive in construction than they need be-after all, they are only for use for a few years-and should be of a more temporary nature, and that a great deal of lumber and building material is being wasted in them, and also much labour is required which would be very useful in building homes and doing other construction work. Are all the plans made and passed in the air department alone, or is there some other department which checks to see that they are not too extravagant?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not know that there is any other department which checks them. We have a works and buildings development committee, composed of officers of our department, who go over the plans and specifications of every one of these buildings. There is no other department which checks; I do not see how there could be. The plans and specifications are submitted to the chief engineer, works and buildings-
In the minister's department?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
In our department. We have a branch of works and buildings. Then it goes to the deputy minister, and eventually comes to me for the financial encumbrance necessary to raise the money to put up the building. I think most of the equipment depots are on a model of some kind. In some places they
(Mr. Power.]
may be greater in scope than in others, but I think the model is there; the type of building is one for which specifications were laid down some time ago. My hon. friend is thinking, perhaps, of the equipment depot in 'Vancouver. A lot of stuff has to go in there.

I simply use the equipment depots as an illustration. Hundreds of millions of dollars are being spent each year on buildings by the Department of National Defence and apparently there is nobody to check them. Contractors have come to me and said it is ridiculous that the buildings should be of the type they are, that they are costing far more than they should; and it seems to me that some of the buildings I have observed in process of going up are far bigger than are required for the number of men who are to use them. Of course I am not an expert on the subject, but I think there should be some check, probably by the Department of Finance, on these plans and on the amount of money which is going into buildings most of which will be absolutely useless once the war is over. I believe the country is losing millions of dollars in this way.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I do not think the Department of Finance has at its disposal a corps of engineers or any thoroughly qualified person 

a constructor or engineer or somebody like that-for purposes of checking. We go to treasury board or to council with an appropriation for so much money to build an equipment depot or some other building, but I am sure the Minister of Finance of his own knowledge cannot know whether I am building too extravagant a building or one which is too ornate for the purpose. I do not know how checking could be done other than by superimposing a corps of engineers over all construction, including that of the Department of Public Works.
During the war would it not be wise to have some board of that kind set up in the Department of Finance?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
So far as we are concerned it would not be of much use. We are practically finished. We are spending 39 millions this year on all these plans which are now in, and I imagine it would be more trouble than it would be worth to change the plans. Specifications have been drawn for everything we propose to build. If we have to put up a new school, we have the type of buildings which go with each school, so many buildings, so many feet long, so many feet high and so many feet wide, to accommodate so many people. The specifications are laid down for the mess hall, recreation hall, and so on; the hangar

War Appropriation-Air Services
is so big, or it is a double hangar. All that kind of thing is just a matter of taking the blueprint out of a drawer and going ahead with it, in any normal construction that we require.
The point is a very serious one because of the difficulties in building homes across the country.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will admit to my hon. friend that, in the hurry to get things done, put up buildings and have our schools going, perhaps at the start there may have been some lack of supervision. I was camping on the trail of these engineers to get the buildings built, the schools opened, and if they have spent a little more money than they need to have done I suppose I must take the blame for it. But now it is standardized, and I do not know how money could be saved unless we had a committee of some kind going all through every type of building we have and checking up on it.
I believe there could yet be quite a saving on buildings to be erected in the future.

In connection with this amount, which almost parallels the previous year's expenditures, could we have information as to more recent developments, with particular reference to the middle western provinces, and the amounts which have been or will be spent on totally new projects?

The discussion has been very lively for the last few minutes, but perhaps we are still in the dark. Personally I do not expect the Minister of National Defence for Air to be able to answer every question in regard to the building programme of his department, and I will tell the committee why. I think it is generally recognized that the purchase of land, the letting of building contracts, the supplying of materials and so forth come under the Department of Munitions and Supply. I point out at this time, and suggest to the minister that I may elaborate upon it further when the estimates of the Department of Munitions and Supply come up, that I think it will be discovered that the engineers, perhaps the architects and others who come into the picture at the commencement of any building operation, have erred in their plans and their judgment too many times, with the result that when construction has been completed something has been found to be faulty or something has been discovered which has put the government to tremendous expense in connection with some mistake or something unforeseen which should have been discovered by the engineers or those responsible for letting the contract in the first place. [The Chairman.]

If the minister wishes to take the responsibility for what I have in mind he may do so, but I doubt very much if he will be able to tell us why certain things happened. I shall give him a specific case, and perhaps the Minister of Munitions and Supply will deal with it when his department comes on. A certain air training school was located at a certain place.
Name?

It was the air training school at Vulcan in Alberta. This is a large school; the buildings are well constructed, and I have no hesitation in saying that it is a fine location as far as appearances go. But when the school was located there and the construction completed they discovered that they did not have enough water to supply the school. Of course at first sight one would say that surely the engineers would have discovered that, because that is why they are sent out there. But they did not discover it. The result has been that they have had to dig huge ditches and put in huge pipes-pipes which could be used for other purposes in our war effort-in order to bring that water for a considerable distance, not yards but miles. If my memory serves me aright, that water has to be pumped about ten miles.
I mention that only as one instance. I do not know how often these things happen throughout the country. I am not offering severe criticism at the moment; I am using this only as an illustration. Surely we should have engineers capable of discovering these things before a project is commenced, and I might add that the particular project to which I have referred was not one of the early ones; it was completed only recently. Surely by this time the engineers should have learned that one of the essential things in connection with an air school is an adequate water supply.
Another matter to which I should like to direct the minister's attention has to do with the salvaging of materials after the construction of a school has been completed. I believe I can say-and the minister can correct me if I am wrong-that there is nothing salvaged after construction work is completed; that the contractors themselves will sell that material and that the government will not receive any benefit from the sale of it. How much it amounts to, I do not know; it may not amount to much. On the other hand it may amount to a great deal. I do not know whether a check is made of how much material is necessary for a building, but I do know that these air training schools are well built.

I have no complaint about that; they should be well built. There is a tremendous amount of material used in them, and also a tremendous amount left over when a building is completed.
I moved for a return some time ago in which I asked the names of those who had bid on salvage, together with any offers accepted. The only offers made were in respect of old buildings on the locations-farm houses and barns. I shall have more to say on that point later on. I know for a fact, however, that much of that material was sold. I know it because I know the people who bought it. The return did not indicate that the government had received payment for that material. How much it might have been, I do not know, nor do I know how much it was sold for.

The agreement is dated June 5, 1942, and covers the administration of Royal Air Force schools in Canada. It amends and extends the British commonwealth air training plan. I quote from page 14 of appendix 2 as follows:
The R.A.F. units in Canada will he administered by the Royal Canadian Air Force in the same manner as units constituted under the British commonwealth air training plan, provided that:
(i)	they will preserve their R.A.F. identity.
