Such arrangements may be varied by agreement between the governments of the United Kingdom and Canada, as required by circumstances.

I think one of the first things that should be taken into consideration when deciding on an airport is the available water supply. Before any development is carried on at all, it should be definitely decided whether a water supply is available. However, that is not what I rose to speak about. I do not know whether the minister will be able to answer this question, but it has to do with airports. I have received certain correspondence from the amalgamated building workers of Canada, Calgary unit No. 1, which is located at the supply depot. It would appear that the cost of living bonus is paid to civilian carpenters working on this job, while the carpenters who are in the civil service, although at one time they did receive this bonus, are not being paid a bonus. This creates a good deal of hard feeling. At first the government employees received a cost of living bonus of three cents an hour, but this was stopped and since that time the 'bonus that was paid has been collected back. I will read a portion of the letter I received, as follows:
Cost of living bonus to civilian employees of the R.C.A.F. in all commands has been paid in accordance with the provisions of R.C. 6702, of August 26, 1941.
When the bonus was paid there was no objection. The letter continues:
In July, 1942, on receipt of Department of Labour correction sheet authorizing wage payment of ninety-five cents per hour plus cost of living bonus of three cents per hour to carpenters in Calgary and zone, a direction was issued in error by the air officer commanding No. 4 air training command, that wages and bonus were to be paid at such rate effective from August 1, 1942.
Later on not only was the bonus cut off, but the government is charging the employees for the overpayment. The net result is that they do not receive the bonus and are having to pay back that which they did receive, and
the civilian employees are still being paid' this bonus. There is a difference in wages to men who are doing the same type of work. I understand that a conference was to be called in an effort to bring about some uniformity in the wages paid to the civil service employees and the civilian employees. I will read another portion of this letter dated May 18, 1943, which I received from the treasury office, so that the minister will see exactly what has happened. I quote:
This department has had occasion previously to consult with the national war labour board regarding the difference in bonus payable to employees of the public service and those of private industry. We were advised some months ago that the situation had become so confused that a conference was being arranged with government departments and agencies concerned with the intention of establishing a uniform procedure which would result in equalizing bonus rates and payments to all civilian employees engaged in the same type of work in the same district or zone. However, to date no such conference has taken place so far as we are aware and until such conference is arranged and direction given this department has no alternative but to pay bonus to prevailing rate employees in accordance with bonus payment procedure previously laid down.
Apparently the question, has risen on many occasions; the department is cognizant of that disparity, and there are hopes that something may be done. But they say that a conference was expected to be called. May I ask whether that conference was ever called?

My officers do not think much of the suggestion. The medical officers of the department say that to a larger extent than was indicated by the hon. member for Renfrew South there is an air specialty, a special need for medical work in research and elsewhere in relation to the air force. I have sent over to my hon. friend' some pamphlets prepared by our medical services. These have been prepared and printed in this expensive

way-I show them to my hon. friend now-by the insurance companies of Canada, for distribution among the civilians of Canada. Here is one entitled, "What they eat to be fit is good for the health of all Canadians." I think this would indicate that in nutrition we are considerably in advance of the ordinary civilian medical practitioner. Our medical officers have gone into nutrition in its relation to flying. They have studied, for instance, what effect riboflavin has on eyesight. That has been carefully studied and many experiments have been made in connection with it. An hon. member spoke of films the other day. We have developed a film based on this training pamphlet. It has been shown recently in the United States. It was shown first of all to our own people and then to insurance executives throughout the country, and recently it was shown in Toronto to the executives of the Twentieth Century Fox Corporation, Famous Players and others. I have received this letter from the head of Famous Players Canadian Corporation wdiich I think would be of interest to put on the record:
We are of the unanimous opinion that this subject, which is so well done^-
It was done by ourselves in association with Associated Screen News.
-can be of inestimable value to the health of Canadian citizens and suggest that, if possible, the R.C.A.F. make the film available for motion picture theatres so that it can be shown to the civilian population throughout Canada.
We think so well of this subject that Famous Players, as a theatre operating company and as a service to the Canadian public, would cheerfully pay for the printing of the necessary positive film in colour to make this subject available for the theatres of Canada. To get proper coverage this would require 12 positive prints. Also, we would order one 35 mm. print in colour which would be delivered to the R.C.A.F. for use as they see fit.
Famous Players operate or have an interest in approximately 340 theatres having a total seating capacity of about 310,000. However, it is not our intention that the film should be shown exclusively in our theatres but it should be made available for all theatres in Canada that wish to show it and we estimate that during the life of this film it will be shown to somewhere around five million people.
Paramount Film Service of Canada have volunteered to distribute this film without charge and Canadian theatre owners generally will be advised through the Canadian Motion Picture Trade papers that this picture will be available for use in their theatres by applying to Paramount Film Service.
That w'as a specialty, nutrition, developed by our Royal Canadian Air Force Medical Service. We have also gone into other spheres, particularly pressure chamber work, blackouts-human black-outs-and things of that

kind. Our people really think they are doing a good job in their particular line, and I do not believe they would be keen on changing over to the army, where a good many of them came from.

I should like to call to the attention of the committee the service that is being rendered, by the Red' Cross society in the building up of blood banks. I do not believe there is any other contribution that the Red Cross is making to our war effort which is of more value than the blood banks. I believe the minister will corroborate me when I say that they are being used extensively not only in the air force but in the other two branches of the armed services.
Let me give one specific case. A young pilot officer whom I happen to know was shot down over the Mediterranean while serving in the defence of Malta. He was rushed to hospital in Malta, and one of the first things done for him was to pump blood plasma into his system. There is no doubt that this saved his life. Altogether he had fifteen pints of blood pumped into his system, of which six were of the plasma type collected by the Red Cross. My reason for mentioning that at this time is that I believe there are a great many right here in this House of Commons who would volunteer to give their blood to-morrow if they knew how simple the process was, and go to the Ottawa Red Cross on Metcalfe street. I happen to be a donor, and I can tell the committee frankly that it does not hurt any more to have your blood taken than it does to prick your finger; in fact, apart from having an abnormal thirst, you feel better afterwards than before you go in.
The hon. member for Peterborough West mentioned the efficacy of the sulfa drugs. I believe that blood plasma ranks in importance with the sulfa drugs in saving lives.
I agree with the hon. member on that.

All hon. members between the ages of twenty-one and sixty years who weigh over 120 pounds and whose blood is up to the proper standard can donate their blood. I know of no greater contribution that they can make to the armed forces of Canada than by becoming blood donors with the Canadian Red Cross.

I am pleased that the hon. member for Leeds brought this matter up, because I know that in the army everything possible is being done to enable men to go to the blood donors' clinics. I have not heard what is being done
in the air force, but I trust that the ground crews, at least, will be able to go to the clinics.
Does the minister know what the findings were in regard to the investigation at No. 35 elementary flying training school, where one man died following toxoid inoculation, on May 19, and a number of others were in the hospital?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I saw an item in the paper on this matter and have made inquiries. When I last asked, yesterday or the day before, the inquiries were not quite completed. I do know that quite an investigation is going on. A man, whose name I think is Fraser, from the Connaught laboratories of Toronto, also the deputy minister of health for Manitoba, Dr. Jackson, and some other prominent civilians, went out to make inquiries. We are having an inquiry of our own, but I do not think it is completed. It looks as though the incident is one which needs to be thoroughly investigated; one man died and about thirty were laid up as a result of inoculation. Whether the blame is to be ascribed to the persons who did the inoculating, or whether there was something wrong with the material, or whether the incident is the result of some other circumstance, I have not yet been able to ascertain.
That is what I wish to find out.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes; I have the matter very much in mind.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In connection with the clothing of the air force, I notice that there is a change in certain branches as far as summer uniform is concerned. Does that apply as well to the women's division?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes. We are going to have another summer uniform. It is out, but I have not seen it yet.

Are the members of the Royal Canadian Air Force who are going on night operations given vitamin A tablets? I believe these tablets are provided in some parts of the United States, also in Great Britain, in large doses.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not know. I will find out. I know we are doing our best to see that the eyesight of our men is improved and that they are generally in good condition. I do not know whether vitamin A is what is used.

Vitamin A is supposed to cure night blindness and also a certain amount of colour blindness.

War Appropriation-Air Services

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: This new drug, riboflavin is, I believe, supposed to be good for this purpose. I do not know what it is.
It is administered in 50,000 international units.
Would the minister give the reason for such a decided decrease in the estimated expenditure?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes; we bought a lot of clothing and boots last year and our requirements are provided for well in advance.

Why the increase?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There is a very big increase in our communication system for the purposes of defence along both coasts largely for what they call fighter control and for land line communication. I think it is eight miles on the Pacific coast and ten miles on the east coast, and is for wireless communications and fighter control facilities.

I believe that in April of last year-I have not the date here-I asked the minister about carrier pigeons. I think that comes under this vote. He refused to answer because it was not in the country's interest.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Oh; we have carrier pigeons, lots of them.
Then, on August 15, a Toronto paper publishes nearly a full page of information about carrier pigeons. Could the minister tell the committee-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Did I say last year, that we did not want them?
No. The minister said it was not in the country's interest-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: -to have carrier pigeons?
Carrier pigeons, yes.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: To disclose whether we had them or not? *
To tell the house anything about the matter.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Someone must have just told me I should not; that is all. We have certainly given a lot of publicity to it since.

I do not know why I said that. I might have had a reason. Some of my officers must have told me it should not be disclosed, but I cannot understand why I agreed with them.
Could the minister tell us whether all the instruments used, coming under this item, are of Canadian make?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I could not say. I would not think so. This is largely for wires and wireless.
A great deal of equipment comes under it.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes; there is a lot of equipment. I could not give the information now. Of course I can find out. Some equipment may be bought from the United States; some may come from England; but a good part of this is for poles and wires, where it happens to be land line communications, and some is probably in construction, where wires and different communication systems have to come into a sector, or whatever you call it, in this fighter control.

My reason for asking the question was that it may be that some of these instruments are made by one of the capital companies which have been set up, and in that case what I should like to find out is whether the capital companies come into competition either with Canadian companies . whose lifework it is to make these instruments, or with instruments which are brought in from other countries.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring to scientific research?
That is it.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I visited the place once. It is really under my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply, as the hon. member knows, but I gathered from conversation there that they do not compete with anybody in this country; that it is pretty nearly all new gadgets which they are making. But I would not be sure about that. That is a company set up by the Minister of Munitions and Supply.

The question I have in mind is one which, if the minister does not object, I will ask on this item relating to clothing. Have any tests been made as to the relative efficiency of shearling and wool clothing? Shearling is the skin of the animal with the fur on it; and the woven wool clothing is the other. There has been quite a controversy. It happens that there is a plant manufacturing it in my constituency.

Questions
Would the minister ask his officers to see if there is any opinion, in the air force on the relative merits of the two? The question has been brought up to me several times.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will do so with pleasure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not want to prevent the item from being carried, but I wish the minister would take an opportunity over the week-end to look up some information for me on a matter which came to my attention only after other items had been passed, so -that I was not able to ask about it then. The suggestion has come from one who is interested in the chaplain service of the air force that some change might profitably be made in connection with the position which the chaplains hold. I am told that they are not in the same position as ordinary officers. I do not know whether this condition applies to all three of the services. I believe they hold some kind of honorary appointment rather than the ordinary position of an officer. I received that complaint by letter this afternoon and I was wondering if the minister would look into it.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They are honorary officers and they always have been, and the same situation exists in the army. In the navy they have no rank at all, being just chaplains; they are not captains or lieutenant commanders or anything of that kind. However, there must be something in the way of complaint if my hon. friend says so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes. My correspondent
was complaining about that condition. He has been himself in the past an officer, a chaplain officer in the air force-I am not sure-and he complains that there should be no distinction. He states that the chaplains are rendering a great service to the army, the navy and the air force, and there is no reason why they should be called honorary captain or honorary major as the case may be. He thinks they should be in the same position as the others. ,

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I am	under	the	impression
that that has been so from time immemorial.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I	think	that	is so,	butperhaps the minister	will	look	into	the
matter.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They are only honorary. Does my hon. friend want a decision as to whether we will change the system? I cannot change it between now and Monday. I will look into it.
